glance: Cane juice roughly 20–40 BDT per glass
Roadside juice stalls and village markets around Joypurhat town
joypurhat-akher-gur.desc: Sugarcane is everywhere in Joypurhat, and alongside the mill, small village presses crush cane for juice and jaggery. Fresh juice is sold from roadside stalls, sometimes with lime and ginger. In winter some farmers boil the juice in shallow pans to make golden akher gur, which is used in sweets, pitha and tea. It tastes milder than date palm molasses but has its own fresh sweetness.
blocks: Good to know
Choose stalls that press the cane in front of you and use clean ice.

glance: 250 km to Joypurhat by road, 7–8 hours by bus or car
gopinathpur-temple.desc: Gopinathpur Temple lies in the countryside east of Akkelpur and is dedicated to Gopinath, a form of Krishna. Local history links its founding to an endowment from the Bengal Sultanate period, and the temple has been repaired several times since an earthquake in the late 19th century. The surrounding grounds come alive during the yearly fair, when devotees and traders arrive from across the region. On ordinary days it is a calm place to see village temple life.
blocks: How to get there
From Akkelpur upazila town (south of Joypurhat), take a CNG or auto-rickshaw about 6–7 km east.
Good to know
Remove shoes before entering the temple area.

gopinathpur-mela.desc: Each year the grounds around the Gopinathpur temple host a fair that has run for generations. Devotees come for worship, while stalls sell sweets, toys, pottery, household goods and farm tools. For many families in the district it is a social event as much as a religious one, a chance to meet relatives and shop. It is a good window into village fair culture in North Bengal.
blocks: How to get there
As for the temple: via Akkelpur, then a short CNG ride east.
Good to know
Confirm the date locally, as it follows the Hindu lunar calendar. Expect heavy crowds and keep valuables secure.

glance: 250 km to Joypurhat by road, 7–8 hours by bus or car
joypurhat-sugar-mill.desc: Joypurhat Sugar Mill, established in the early 1960s, is the biggest sugar mill in the country and shapes the rhythm of the district's farming year. During the crushing season, roughly from late autumn into winter, bullock carts, tractors and trucks loaded with cane line the roads leading to the mill. The surrounding fields of tall green cane are a characteristic sight of the area. Visitors usually see it from outside, as access to the factory floor needs permission.
blocks: How to get there
On the edge of Joypurhat town; a short rickshaw ride from the centre.
Good to know
Go during the crushing season to see the cane traffic. Ask in advance if you hope to go inside.

glance: 250 km to Joypurhat by road, 7–8 hours by bus or car
nandail-dighi.desc: Like many places in the Barind region, Joypurhat is dotted with large excavated ponds known as dighis, dug long ago by local rulers for water. Nandail Dighi in Kalai is one of the best known in the district. Its banks make a pleasant walk in the cool months, with birds on the water and farmers passing by. It is a simple, restful stop rather than a grand sight.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus or CNG from Joypurhat town to Kalai, then a local auto-rickshaw.
Good to know
Late afternoon light is best; carry snacks as facilities are limited.

glance: 250 km to Joypurhat by road, 7–8 hours by bus or car
lakma-rajbari.desc: Lakma Rajbari is the ruin of a zamindar family's residence close to the western border in Panchbibi upazila. Its brick walls, arched doorways and broken rooms are slowly being reclaimed by trees and creepers. There is no museum or signage, just the building and the surrounding villages and fields. It appeals to travellers who enjoy quiet, unrestored places.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus to Panchbibi from Joypurhat town, then hire an auto-rickshaw towards the border villages.
Good to know
It is close to the border; carry ID and do not stray towards the boundary. The structure is fragile, so stay out of damaged rooms.

glance: Local hotels and home-style eateries in Joypurhat town; fresh runners in town markets
lotiraj-kochu.desc: Lotiraj is a taro variety whose long, soft runners (loti) are the prized part, and Joypurhat has made it a symbol of the district. The runners are cooked with shrimp or small fish, or with mustard and green chilli, into a thick, comforting dish. Fields of large taro leaves are common around Joypurhat, and the produce is sent across Bangladesh and even abroad. It is everyday home food rather than restaurant fare.
blocks: Good to know
Properly cooked kochu should not itch the throat; local cooks add lemon or tamarind to prevent it.

glance: 250 km to Joypurhat by road, 7–8 hours by bus or car
hinda-kasba-shahi-mosque.desc: This mosque stands in Hinda village in Khetlal upazila, about 15 km from Joypurhat town. It was built in the late 1950s under the guidance of a Chishti pir, Abdul Gafur Chishti, and follows Mughal shapes. What makes it special is the outside: instead of terracotta, the walls are covered in mosaics of broken glass and china that sparkle in the sun. It has five domes, built without iron rods, and a 40-foot minaret on the north side.
blocks: How to get there
Take a CNG or bus from Joypurhat towards Khetlal and on to Hinda village.
Good to know
Come in the morning or late afternoon when sunlight makes the mosaic shine. Avoid prayer times.
